title: Arrays & Linked Lists
tagline: Two fundamental ways to store a sequence — and why the tradeoff changes everything about speed.

sections.content:
Long before languages gave us `Array`, `ArrayList`, `Vec`, or `list`, every programmer faced the same raw question: **how do I store an ordered collection of things in memory?** Two fundamentally different answers emerged, and every sequence data structure built since is a variation or combination of them.

The **array** makes one bold upfront bet: reserve a contiguous block of memory large enough for all your elements. In return for that commitment, you get the ability to reach any element in a single arithmetic step — O(1) random access, no matter how large the collection grows. The **linked list** refuses to make that bet. Instead, each element is wrapped in a **node** that lives wherever the allocator finds space, and each node carries a pointer to the next one. You pay for that freedom with traversal cost — reaching the kth element requires walking k hops from the front.

Neither choice is universally better. Arrays win when you need fast random access and cache-friendly iteration. Linked lists win when you need O(1) insertion and deletion at known positions without shifting any elements. The entire discipline of choosing the right data structure reduces, in large part, to understanding this one tradeoff deeply.

This chapter builds that understanding from the ground up: how contiguous memory actually works, why the cache loves arrays, how dynamic resizing achieves amortised O(1) appends, how pointer-chaining enables flexible insertion, what doubly linked lists add, and which real systems choose which structure and why. By the end you will be able to read a problem statement and immediately reason about which structure fits — and defend that choice in a technical interview.

sections.title: Reserved Cinema Seats vs a Treasure Hunt
sections.content:
Picture a cinema with seats numbered 1 through 500. You book seats 101 through 120 — twenty consecutive seats. To reach your friend in seat 114 you walk to row 10, count across to seat 14: one calculation, zero searching. That is an **array**: elements occupy consecutively numbered memory addresses, so the CPU computes the exact address of any element in a single arithmetic step.

Now imagine a treasure hunt. Each envelope you find contains a clue and a map to the next envelope. Envelope 1 tells you envelope 2 is under the park bench. Envelope 2 says envelope 3 is in the library. To reach envelope 7 you must follow the entire chain — no shortcuts exist. That is a **linked list**: each node holds its value and a pointer (the map) to the next node.

The cinema metaphor also reveals insertion cost. Suppose you need to add a seat between seats 112 and 113. The only honest solution is to ask every person from seat 113 onwards to shift one seat to the right — a chain reaction touching every person behind the insertion point. In a linked list, inserting a new envelope between envelope 3 and envelope 4 is trivial: update two pointers. Nobody moves. The treasure hunt wins at insertion; the cinema wins at access.

sections.title: How Arrays Work — Contiguous Memory and Index Arithmetic
sections.content:
An array is a **contiguous block of memory** divided into equal-sized slots, one slot per element. Every element occupies exactly the same number of bytes — determined by the type being stored. An array of 32-bit integers uses 4 bytes per slot; an array of 64-bit floats uses 8.

The operating system hands the program a **base address** — the memory address of the zeroth element. To access element at index `i`, the CPU performs one multiplication and one addition:

`address(i) = base + i × element_size`

This single arithmetic expression is why array access is O(1). It does not matter whether `i` is 0 or 10,000,000 — the calculation takes the same number of CPU cycles. There is no searching, no traversal, no recursion. The hardware executes this as a single **load** instruction.

A **static array** declares its size at creation time. The runtime allocates exactly that many bytes and nothing more. If you need more space, you are stuck — you must allocate a new, larger block and copy every element across. This copy is O(n): you touch every element once.

The rigidity of static arrays is acceptable in low-level languages (C arrays, Rust arrays on the stack) where you either know the size in advance or deliberately manage memory. In most higher-level languages you use dynamic arrays instead.

sections.title: Dynamic Arrays — Automatic Resizing and Amortised Cost
sections.content:
A **dynamic array** (JavaScript `Array`, Python `list`, Java `ArrayList`, Rust `Vec`, C++ `vector`) wraps a static array in logic that automatically grows it when needed. The internal layout is still a contiguous block, but the block is **pre-allocated with extra capacity** beyond what is currently used.

When you `push` an element:
1. If `length < capacity`, write the element into the next slot and increment `length`. O(1).
2. If `length === capacity`, allocate a new block — typically **2× the current capacity** — copy all existing elements into it, write the new element, and update internal pointers. O(n) for this one operation.

The key insight is **how rarely the O(n) copy happens**. After a copy that creates a buffer of capacity `C`, the next `C/2` pushes are all O(1). The next copy doubles to `2C`, costing O(C). Then `C` more O(1) pushes. Then a copy costing O(2C). Summing over n total pushes:

Total copy work ≤ 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + … + n = 2n − 1

Divide by n pushes: **average (amortised) cost per push is O(1)**. A few operations pay dearly; the vast majority are cheap. The total bill is linear even though individual operations vary wildly.

The 2× growth factor is a practical choice. Smaller factors (say 1.5×) reduce wasted memory at the cost of more frequent copies. Larger factors waste more memory. Python uses a sequence closer to 1.125× for very large lists; Java `ArrayList` uses exactly 1.5×. JavaScript engines are implementation-defined but all guarantee amortised O(1) push.

**Insertion and deletion in the middle** break the amortised argument. Inserting at index `k` requires shifting elements at indices `k, k+1, …, length-1` each one slot to the right — O(n) in the worst case (inserting at the front). `Array.prototype.unshift(value)` in JavaScript is O(n) for exactly this reason, even though `push` is O(1) amortised.

sections.title: Why Caches Love Arrays
sections.content:
Modern CPUs don't fetch memory one byte at a time — they fetch **cache lines**, typically 64 bytes at a stretch. When you read `array[0]`, the hardware automatically loads `array[0]` through roughly `array[15]` (for 4-byte integers) into the L1 cache. Accessing `array[1]` through `array[15]` is then essentially free — they are already sitting in the fastest memory the machine has.

This property is called **spatial locality**: adjacent memory addresses are likely to be accessed together. Arrays have perfect spatial locality because elements are literally adjacent in memory.

Linked list nodes, by contrast, are scattered across the heap — allocated at different times in different places. Reading `node.next` triggers a pointer dereference to an unpredictable address. The cache line loaded for `node` is unlikely to contain the next node. Each traversal step may cause a **cache miss**, forcing the CPU to reach out to slower L2 or L3 cache, or even main RAM (DRAM).

On modern hardware, a cache hit takes ~4 cycles; an L3 miss takes ~40 cycles; a DRAM access takes ~200 cycles. For large linked lists, this difference completely dominates theoretical algorithmic complexity. A sequential scan over a million-element array often outperforms the same scan over a million-node linked list **by 5–10×** in practice, even though both are O(n) in the Big-O sense.

This is why systems code — parsers, database engines, game loops — almost always prefer arrays or array-like structures over linked lists for sequential processing, even when the algorithmic complexity is identical.

sections.title: Linked List Fundamentals — Nodes and Pointers
sections.content:
A **singly linked list** stores each element in a **node** — a small object with two fields:
- `value`: the data being stored
- `next`: a reference (pointer) to the next node, or `null` for the last node

The list tracks a `head` reference pointing to the first node. Traversal walks from `head` through `next` pointers until reaching `null`. Reading element at index `i` visits `i + 1` nodes — O(n).

But **insertion and deletion** look completely different from arrays. To insert a new node between nodes A and B:
1. Create the new node `N`.
2. Set `N.next = B`
3. Set `A.next = N`

Two pointer writes. O(1). No shifting. No copying. The rest of the list is completely undisturbed. This is the linked list's great strength: once you have a reference to the insertion point, the structural change is O(1).

The catch hidden in that phrase is **"once you have a reference"**. Getting to position `k` still costs O(k). Linked lists do not help with random access — they help with insertion and deletion **by reference**, which is a very different guarantee.

A list without a **tail pointer** must traverse to the end to append — O(n). Simply storing a `tail` reference alongside `head` turns append into O(1): create node, set `tail.next = node`, update `tail = node`. This is an essential optimisation that is easy to overlook in first implementations.

sections.title: Doubly Linked Lists — Bidirectional Traversal and O(1) Deletion
sections.content:
A **doubly linked list** augments each node with a `prev` pointer in addition to `next`. The list typically stores both `head` and `tail` references. This seemingly small addition has significant consequences.

**Backward traversal** becomes possible: from any node you can walk toward the head. This is used in editors (undo history), browsers (back/forward page history), and music players (previous track).

**O(1) deletion by reference** — this is the killer feature. In a singly linked list, deleting a node whose reference you hold still requires knowing its predecessor. Finding the predecessor means walking from `head`: O(n). With `prev`, you already know the predecessor — it is `node.prev`. Deletion becomes:

```
node.prev.next = node.next
node.next.prev = node.prev  (if node.next exists)
```

Two pointer writes. O(1) — even in the middle of the list.

This property is exploited in the **LRU (Least Recently Used) cache**, one of the most common system design interview questions. The cache uses a doubly linked list plus a hash map: the map provides O(1) lookup of any node by key, and the doubly linked list enables O(1) removal and reinsertion at the front (most recently used). The combination achieves O(1) for both `get` and `put` operations.

The price of `prev` pointers: every node stores two pointers instead of one. On a 64-bit system each pointer is 8 bytes, so a doubly linked list of 32-bit integers uses 20 bytes per element (4 for value + 8 for next + 8 for prev) versus 4 bytes per element in an array — five times the memory. For small or sparse lists this is fine; for millions of elements it can matter.

This pattern is the heart of the O(1) LRU cache: the hash map stores node references, and the doubly linked list handles O(1) structural updates. Without `prev` pointers, `deleteNode` would need to walk from `head` to find the predecessor — O(n).

sections.title: The Big-O Comparison Table — Reading the Tradeoffs
sections.content:
Understanding when to reach for each structure requires internalising the complexity table, but more importantly understanding **why** each entry is what it is.

**Access by index** — Arrays: O(1) (arithmetic); Linked lists: O(n) (traversal). This is the fundamental distinction from which everything else follows.

**Insert at front** — Arrays: O(n) because every existing element must shift one slot right to create space at index 0. Linked lists: O(1) — create a node, point it at the current head, update `head`. The rest of the list is untouched.

**Insert at back** — Dynamic arrays: O(1) amortised (the doubling argument from earlier). Linked lists with tail pointer: O(1). Without tail pointer: O(n). This is a tie when both are implemented correctly.

**Insert in the middle** — Both: O(n). Arrays need O(n) shifts; linked lists need O(n) traversal to reach the position (though the actual splice is O(1) once there).

**Delete by reference (given a node/pointer)** — Arrays: O(n) to shift elements. Singly linked list: O(n) to find the predecessor. **Doubly linked list: O(1)** — the `prev` pointer gives direct access to the predecessor.

**Search (unsorted)** — Both: O(n). No structure helps with unsorted sequential search.

**Memory per element** — Array: just the element bytes (tight, cache-friendly). Singly linked list: element + one pointer. Doubly linked list: element + two pointers. On 64-bit systems, two pointers = 16 extra bytes per node.

The practical upshot: if your workload is dominated by random access and iteration, use an array. If your workload is dominated by insertion and deletion at specific known positions (like a text editor's cursor position, a playlist's current-song marker, or an LRU cache eviction), use a doubly linked list with a supplementary hash map for O(1) lookup.

The timing comparison between `push` and `unshift` makes the O(n) shift cost viscerally real: both call the same-looking array method, but their complexity is night-and-day different.

sections.title: Classic Linked List Techniques — Reversing, Cycle Detection, Runner Pattern
sections.content:
Linked lists appear heavily in coding interviews because they test **pointer thinking** — the ability to reason about references changing without losing track of the structure. A handful of classic techniques cover the vast majority of interview questions.

**Reversing a singly linked list in-place** is the archetypal exercise. The naive approach might copy values into an array and write them back, but that uses O(n) extra space. The in-place approach uses three pointers — `prev`, `curr`, `next` — and rewires the chain one node at a time in O(n) time and O(1) space:

```
prev = null, curr = head
while curr is not null:
    next = curr.next        // save next before overwriting
    curr.next = prev        // flip the arrow
    prev = curr             // advance prev
    curr = next             // advance curr
head = prev                 // prev is now the new head
```

**Cycle detection (Floyd's tortoise and hare)** solves the problem of detecting a loop in a linked list without using extra memory. Maintain two pointers: `slow` moves one step at a time, `fast` moves two steps. If there is a cycle, `fast` will eventually lap `slow` — they will point to the same node. If `fast` reaches `null`, there is no cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space.

**The runner (two-pointer) pattern** generalises: maintain two pointers at different speeds or offsets. To find the **middle** of a list, start both at `head` and advance `fast` by 2 and `slow` by 1 — when `fast` hits the end, `slow` is at the middle. To find the **kth node from the end**, advance `fast` k steps ahead, then move both at the same pace — when `fast` hits the end, `slow` is at the kth-from-last node.

These patterns appear because linked lists prevent random access, forcing you to extract information through careful coordinated traversal.

sections.title: Real-World Usage — When Each Structure Appears in Production
sections.content:
Understanding where these structures appear in real systems deepens intuition for when to reach for each.

**Arrays (and dynamic arrays) are everywhere by default:**
- **Database rows** returned by a query come back as an array of records. Sequential scan is the dominant access pattern, perfectly matching array cache behaviour.
- **Pixel buffers** for images and video: a 1920×1080 RGB image is exactly a contiguous array of 6,220,800 bytes. Any other representation would make the GPU unhappy.
- **Ring buffers** (circular arrays) underpin audio processing, networking I/O, and producer-consumer queues. A fixed-size array with head and tail indices achieves O(1) enqueue and dequeue with zero allocation.
- **Stack and queue implementations** in most languages default to dynamic arrays with amortised O(1) push/pop.

**Linked lists appear in specific high-churn scenarios:**
- **OS process queues and scheduler runqueues** (Linux's CFS scheduler) use red-black trees and linked lists — O(1) splice when moving a process between queues is critical at kernel scheduling frequency.
- **LRU and LFU caches** (Memcached, Redis eviction policies, browser cache) combine a doubly linked list with a hash map for O(1) access and O(1) eviction.
- **JavaScript event loop** maintains a linked list of microtask and macrotask queues internally.
- **Undo/redo history** in text editors: each state change is a node; moving forward and backward is O(1) pointer following.
- **Hash table chaining** — the most common hash collision strategy uses linked lists of colliding entries per bucket. When the bucket list is short (the common case), this is effectively O(1).

**Deque (double-ended queue)** is a hybrid: Python's `collections.deque` is implemented as a **doubly linked list of fixed-size array blocks** (a deque of blocks). This gives O(1) append and pop from both ends while preserving cache locality within each block. This is a textbook example of combining the strengths of both structures.

sections.title: Edge Cases, Common Bugs, and Interview Pitfalls
sections.content:
**Empty list handling** is the most common source of null pointer bugs. Every linked list operation must handle the empty case. `head` is `null`; `tail` is `null`. Both must be updated on the first `append` or `prepend`. Many incorrect implementations update only one of them.

**Off-by-one in index operations** — `insertAt(k, value)` requires walking `k - 1` steps (stopping at the node *before* the insertion point), not `k` steps. Getting this wrong is especially common when `k` equals 0 (insert at front) or equals `length` (insert at back) — both need special-case handling.

**Losing the tail pointer on deletion** — when `deleteNode` removes the current `tail`, the new tail is `tail.prev` (doubly linked) or the penultimate node (singly linked, requires traversal). Forgetting to update `this.tail` leaves the list in a corrupt state where `append` will produce wrong results.

**Circular list confusion** — some problems intentionally create circular lists (the `next` of the last node points back to `head`). Algorithms that blindly walk `while (node.next !== null)` will loop forever. Always clarify whether cycles are possible and add a visited-set or a step counter when they might be.

**Memory leaks in languages without garbage collection** — in C and C++, deleting a node from a linked list does not free the node's memory. The caller must `free(node)` after unlinking it. Forgetting this is a classic C bug.

**Sentinel nodes (dummy heads)** — a common technique to simplify edge cases: add a permanent dummy node at the front (and sometimes back) of the list that never holds real data. With a dummy head, `head.next` is always the first real node. Insertions and deletions at the front no longer need special-case logic — they look the same as operations in the middle. Many clean interview implementations use this pattern.

**Historical context:** Arrays predate high-level languages entirely — early assembly programmers directly computed memory offsets by hand. Linked lists were first formally described by Allen Newell, Cliff Shaw, and Herbert Simon in 1955–1956 as part of the IPL (Information Processing Language), one of the first AI programming languages. The self-referential pointer structure was revolutionary: it meant data structures could reshape themselves at runtime without pre-declaring sizes. John McCarthy's LISP (1958) popularised linked lists as a first-class abstraction — the cons cell (a pair of `car` and `cdr`, essentially `value` and `next`) became the entire foundation of Lisp data representation. The concept of amortised analysis for dynamic arrays was formalised by Robert Tarjan in 1985.

**Interview essentials to have cold:**
- **Reverse a singly linked list** in O(n) time, O(1) space — three pointer iteration, not recursion.
- **Detect a cycle** using Floyd's two-pointer (tortoise and hare) — no extra set needed.
- **Find the middle** of a linked list in one pass — slow/fast pointer, stop when fast reaches null.
- **Merge two sorted linked lists** — the merge step of merge sort, adapted for pointers.
- **Dummy head trick** — eliminates special-casing for empty list or operations at position 0.
- **Common complexity trap**: `Array.unshift` is O(n), not O(1). Interviewers deliberately ask about it.
- **LRU cache design** always combines a doubly linked list with a hash map — be ready to implement both and explain why each is needed.

items: Arrays store elements in **contiguous memory**. The CPU computes `base + i × element_size` in one step, giving O(1) random access for any index, regardless of size.

**Dynamic arrays** (JS Array, Python list, Java ArrayList) auto-resize by doubling capacity on overflow. The total copy work across n pushes is less than 2n, making each push **O(1) amortised** — even though individual copies are O(n).

Arrays have excellent **cache locality**: sequential reads pull entire cache lines (64 bytes) into fast L1/L2 cache. Linked list traversal causes frequent cache misses because nodes are scattered across the heap.

Linked list **insertion and deletion by reference** are O(1) — rewiring two pointers. However, *finding* that position is still O(n). The O(1) benefit only applies when you already hold a reference to the target node.
**Doubly linked lists** add a `prev` pointer, enabling O(1) deletion by reference without predecessor traversal. This is the core mechanism behind O(1) LRU cache eviction.

Use **arrays** for random access, sequential scans, and cache-sensitive workloads. Use **linked lists** (usually doubly linked with a hash map) for frequent O(1) structural modifications at known positions.

Classic linked list interview patterns — reverse in-place, cycle detection (Floyd's), runner/two-pointer, dummy head — all exploit the O(1) pointer-rewire property and avoid the O(n) traversal cost wherever possible.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of accessing element at index `i` in a static array?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: Arrays store elements contiguously. The CPU computes `base + i × element_size` in one arithmetic step — O(1) regardless of array size or the value of i.

quiz.question: Why does appending to a JavaScript Array have O(1) amortised complexity despite occasional O(n) copies?
options: JavaScript engines use a hash map instead of contiguous memory
The buffer doubles on overflow so copies happen exponentially rarely, keeping total copy work below 2n
JavaScript Array uses a linked list under the hood for O(1) appends
The garbage collector handles copying asynchronously, hiding the cost
quiz.explanation: When the buffer fills, a 2× buffer is allocated and all elements copied. Because the buffer doubles, total copy work across n appends is less than 2n — giving O(1) amortised cost per append even though individual copy events are O(n).

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of prepending (inserting at the head) in a singly linked list?
options: O(n) — must traverse to update tail
O(log n)
O(n²)
O(1) — create node, point it at head, update head pointer
quiz.explanation: Prepending creates a new node, sets its `next` to the current head, and updates the `head` reference — three pointer operations independent of list length. O(1).

quiz.question: You hold a direct reference to a node in a doubly linked list. What is the time complexity of deleting that node?
options: O(n) — must find and update predecessor
O(log n)
O(1) — use prev and next pointers to bypass the node
O(n²)
quiz.explanation: The `prev` pointer gives direct access to the predecessor. Deletion updates `node.prev.next = node.next` and `node.next.prev = node.prev` — two pointer writes, O(1). No traversal required.

quiz.question: Which operation is O(n) on a dynamic array but O(1) on a singly linked list?
options: Reading element at index 5
Searching for a specific value
Inserting at the front (prepend)
Appending to the back with a tail pointer
quiz.explanation: Inserting at the front of a dynamic array requires shifting every existing element one position right — O(n). Prepending to a linked list updates only the head pointer — O(1).

quiz.question: Why do linked lists frequently cause more cache misses than arrays during sequential traversal?
options: Linked list nodes are larger than array elements
Node addresses are scattered across the heap, so each next-pointer dereference points to an unpredictable memory location outside the current cache line
Linked lists do not support sequential traversal
The CPU cannot prefetch linked list nodes
quiz.explanation: When the CPU reads an array element it also loads nearby elements into the cache line (64 bytes, ~16 ints). Linked list nodes live at arbitrary addresses, so each node traversal step likely fetches a new cache line from slower memory — causing repeated cache misses.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of `Array.prototype.unshift(value)` in JavaScript?
options: O(1) amortised — same as push
O(log n)
O(n) — shifts every existing element one index right
O(n²)
quiz.explanation: `unshift` must shift every existing element one index to the right to create space at index 0, touching all n elements. O(n) — very different from O(1) amortised `push`.

quiz.question: In a singly linked list with no tail pointer, what is the time complexity of appending to the back?
options: O(log n)
O(n) — must traverse from head to find the last node
O(n²)
quiz.explanation: Without a tail pointer you must walk from head through every next pointer until reaching a node whose `next` is null, then link the new node there. This visits all n existing nodes — O(n).

quiz.question: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm detects a cycle in a linked list using two pointers moving at different speeds. What are its time and space complexities?
options: O(n) time, O(n) space — stores visited nodes in a set
O(n) time, O(1) space — no auxiliary data structure needed
O(n log n) time, O(1) space
O(n²) time, O(1) space — nested pointer comparison
quiz.explanation: The slow pointer advances one step and the fast pointer two steps per iteration. If a cycle exists, fast laps slow and they meet — O(n) time. Only two pointers are needed, so O(1) extra space.

quiz.question: An LRU cache needs O(1) both for `get(key)` and for `put(key, value)` including eviction. Which combination achieves this?
options: A sorted array — binary search gives O(log n) access
A singly linked list — O(1) prepend for most-recent
A doubly linked list plus a hash map — O(1) lookup via map, O(1) move-to-front and eviction via prev/next pointers
A binary search tree — O(log n) access and deletion
quiz.explanation: The hash map gives O(1) node lookup by key. The doubly linked list enables O(1) move-to-front (mark as recently used) and O(1) remove-from-tail (evict least recently used) — because both operations only rewire prev/next pointers on known nodes.
